title.en: He Slapped the Man Who Stole His Mother's Gold Watch—Then the Old Ledger Opened
title.zh: 他掌掴了偷走母亲金表的男人，随后那本旧账簿被打开了

description.en: For eighteen years, Daniel believed Henry Vale was a thief. At the Mercer dinner, the watch returned with a ledger, two recordings and a truth capable of taking the whole estate.
description.zh: 十八年来，Daniel 一直认定 Henry Vale 是个窃贼。默瑟晚宴上，金表与账簿、两段录音一同归来，而真相足以夺走整座庄园。

title.en: The Mercer Dinner: An Old Lie Returned in Gold
title.zh: 默瑟晚宴：披金而归的旧谎言

summary.en: At a glittering Mercer family dinner, Daniel publicly strikes the man blamed for stealing his mother's gold watch—only to learn that the returned heirloom carries eighteen years of evidence against his father, his family and himself.
summary.zh: 在一场华丽的默瑟家宴上，Daniel 当众掌掴了那个被指控偷走母亲金表的男人，却发现这件重归家族的遗物，带回了十八年前关于父亲、家人和他自己的全部证据。

warning.en: Fiction. Contains an on-page slap, minor blood, family manipulation, financial abuse, illness and emotionally intense confrontation.
warning.zh: 虚构故事。包含掌掴、轻微流血、家庭操控、财务侵害、疾病及情绪激烈的对峙情节。

en: ## Chapter One: The Slap Beneath the Chandelier

The crack of Daniel Mercer's slap exploded through the drawing room, sharp enough to silence even the faint clink of crystal. Henry Vale's head snapped sideways. He staggered and struck the ivory sofa with his shoulder, folding over the upholstered back for a moment while the chandelier above them trembled.
Daniel stood over him in a tailored cream suit, breathing hard. "You took a family heirloom that never belonged to you." The room went utterly still.

The vast room had been arranged for a lavish dinner: candlelight warmed the pale walls, a string quartet played beyond the doorway, dark floors framed a light carpet, and the gilded coffee table scattered the chandelier into a thousand points of light. Two suited men stood at the edge of the hall with their drinks lowered. Five minutes earlier they had been discussing the future of the Mercer Foundation; now they looked as though they regretted not leaving with the valet.

Evelyn Mercer sat rigid in a champagne-colored gown, still clutching a glass she had stopped drinking from. Beside her, Daniel's wife Ruth held her own glass motionless on her lap. Henry slowly straightened. A narrow line of blood shone beneath his nose and along the edge of his upper lip.

Daniel's fist remained clenched. Henry neither defended himself nor struck back. He only watched Daniel with the weary composure of a man who had waited years for a particular door to open and had already prepared himself for what would be found behind it.

"You could have asked me," Henry said. Daniel gave a dry, unnatural laugh. He had asked at nineteen, and Henry had told him it was none of his business. "It was my mother's watch," Daniel said. Henry lowered his eyes for half a second, less in guilt than in recognition of the past.

Then Daniel noticed the black gift bag beside the coffee table. It had not been there before. Its stiff handles belonged to the kind of jeweler that made the packaging feel as weighty as the purchase. White tissue rose from the opening, and beneath it a flash of gold caught the chandelier. Daniel's throat tightened.
Henry bent carefully, his knees stiffer than he liked to admit, and lifted the bag. Something shifted softly inside the tissue: gold, rounded, and horribly familiar. The Marlowe pocket watch.

For eighteen years it had been the missing piece in every version of that night. Daniel remembered his mother's birthday dinner, rain beating the windows, Henry leaving through the kitchen door with his coat unbuttoned, and his father standing in the hall with bloodless lips. By morning the watch was gone. By noon, Henry had been named the thief. Malcolm Mercer said it only once, as calmly as though reporting a burst pipe: Henry took it. That was all.
## Chapter Two: The File

There had been no police report, no insurance claim and no confrontation supported by evidence. The accusation settled over the house like dust on old furniture. Now Henry placed the gift bag on the table and reached into his navy jacket. Daniel stepped forward, but Henry produced only a phone.

"Don't try anything," Daniel warned. Henry wiped the blood from his lip, studied it on his thumb and made a call. "Send the file. Now." Around them the evening began to come apart in fragments: a quickened breath, the chime of glass, the quartet stopping in the middle of a phrase. When Daniel demanded to know what file, Henry finished the call and slipped the phone away.

"You always say you want the truth," Henry told him, "but what you want is a version tailored to let you believe your hands are still clean." Ruth saw the fear enter Daniel's eyes beneath the anger. He accused Henry of coming to humiliate them.

Henry looked toward the two men in the hall: a Chicago venture capitalist and the chairman of a preservation trust Daniel had courted for six months. Their money was the estate's best chance of avoiding auction. "I came tonight because you invited half the people who most need to know what your father did." Daniel went rigid. Evelyn set down her glass so quickly that champagne splashed the table. "What did Dad do?" she asked.

Henry's expression softened when he looked at Evelyn. He told her this should not be said here, but Daniel closed the distance across the coffee table and demanded that he say it now. Ruth rose without touching her husband; she knew that when he was trying to prove he could bear everything alone, pulling at him only made him harder.

Henry's phone vibrated. He read the message, tightened his jaw, and placed the phone between the black bag and the abandoned champagne. "Look for yourself." The email held no dramatic subject line, only a scanned document and an audio attachment. Daniel opened the document first. It was a trust ledger.

Daniel knew enough about the family finances to recognize the old Mercer trust insignia. His father had stamped it on everything, even grocery lists. On the yellowed page, three names appeared in blue-black ink: Malcolm Mercer, Henry Vale and Clara Mercer—Daniel's mother.

The ledger recorded an enormous transfer from Clara's family trust into a private account Daniel had never heard of. Evelyn came to stand beside him. Henry explained that Malcolm had drained the trust over three years: some of the money covered debts, some kept the company alive, and some merely allowed a proud man to pretend the family was still rich. Daniel looked up and called it a lie.
## Chapter Three: Three Names in Blue-Black Ink

Henry had expected disbelief. Daniel had always found it easy to hate him. Ruth moved closer and asked the obvious question: why was Henry's name on the ledger? He took a slow breath. "Because I signed the first transfer."

The answer did more damage than any excuse. Henry had been Malcolm's chief financial officer and closest friend. At Daniel's graduation he had given him a leather journal and warned him never to confuse money with power. Daniel had once admired him, which was perhaps why the hatred had gone so deep. "You helped him," Daniel said. Henry agreed. Then he parted the white tissue in the gift bag and revealed the watch.

The watch looked smaller than Daniel remembered: solid gold, oval-faced, with a rounded cover and a fine chain. His grandmother's initials had been engraved on the back decades before his birth. It still carried the mellow shine of old money, the kind that survived wars, divorces and failed investments while persuading its owners that their name could never die.

His mother had carried it in her coat whenever she traveled. Daniel remembered her opening it at breakfast, the faint ticking and the private smile it brought to her face. Henry broke the silence. Malcolm had arranged to sell it to a buyer in Geneva. The money would have hidden another round of debt and purchased a little more time to pretend nothing was wrong.

Daniel accused Henry of beating Malcolm to the theft. Henry admitted taking the watch. Evelyn made a sound halfway between a laugh and a sob, and Daniel dug his fingers into the edge of the table. "Then you are still a thief."

Henry held his gaze. He had removed the watch from the safe before Malcolm could sell it, but he had not acted alone. Clara had begged him to do it. For eighteen years Daniel had shaped the past into something he could carry: Henry was the thief, his father the hero trying to save the family, his mother the innocent victim, and Daniel the powerless son. Simple stories were easier to survive. This one was no longer simple. Clara had already known the trust was being emptied, and Henry said she had tried to tell her children.

Malcolm told everyone Clara was confused. He blamed her medication, her memory and exhaustion; he repeated it to doctors, lawyers and anyone who found believing him convenient. Evelyn went pale. Their mother had been ill then—not dying, but tired in ways twenty-year-old Daniel could not understand. She spent afternoons behind half-drawn curtains, forgot names, and apologized in tears when he missed dinner as though she had spilled wine on the carpet.

Daniel had thought she was fragile. He had not known fragility could be manufactured. When he shouted at Henry for watching Malcolm diminish her, Henry admitted that at first he had helped. He had told himself they were protecting Clara from distress until the excuse made him sick.
## Chapter Four: The One Thing He Saved

His rebellion had been to take the watch—the only thing he could remove without immediately triggering a financial audit. Daniel stared until Henry's voice finally sharpened. Henry had not been brave. He feared Malcolm, feared losing his job, and feared Clara would collapse if she learned how long he had lied to her.

So he stole the watch, hid it and told himself that at least he had preserved one thing. His eyes dropped to the gold. "I saved a damned watch." The confession landed between them like a stone. In the hall, one investor quietly set down his drink. No one asked him—or anyone—to leave. That was the terrible skill of wealthy guests: when disaster arrived, they became invisible while missing nothing.

Daniel picked up the phone and played the audio file beneath the ledger. Static came first. Then the voice of Malcolm Mercer, dead for fourteen months, filled the room. Daniel recognized the brittle patience, the tired superiority, the way even an apology had sounded like a correction.

"I need you to take the watch," Malcolm said. A younger Henry answered that Clara would notice and that Malcolm could not sell it. Malcolm dismissed her as suspicious and insisted he could do what he liked with his own property. Henry replied that it was not his. After a pause, Malcolm laughed almost kindly. "You've taken my salary for fifteen years, Henry. Don't start talking to me about principles now." The recording ended. Somewhere in the dining room, a chair scraped softly across the floor.

Daniel gripped the phone until Ruth took it from him, not to comfort him but to keep him from crushing the screen. Evelyn collapsed onto the sofa. She remembered Clara asking about the watch that night. Their mother had come to her room in a blue robe worn through at the cuffs and asked where Malcolm was.

Then Clara had said, "If Henry comes, don't let your brother think he did something wrong." Evelyn had believed she meant the dinner arrangements. She covered her mouth, horrified by how little she had understood. Ruth reminded her that she had been only seventeen.

Evelyn asked Henry whether he had known they would hate him. He said yes. Had he simply allowed it for eighteen years? Again, yes. For the first time he looked truly old—not the elegant silver-haired executive who made bankers sit straighter, but a man hollowed out by exhaustion.

His wife had been gravely ill then. It was not an excuse, only a fact. He had promised her he would put everything right. He believed that after getting the watch out of the house and stopping Malcolm from selling it, he could return with proof and clean up the damage. Looking at the blood on his thumb, Henry said, "Nothing was clean." Daniel leaned forward under the force of his urge to hit him again, but seized the chair back instead. Henry watched him choose restraint.
## Chapter Five: The Audience Clara Feared

Daniel listed everything Henry should have done: tell them, call the police, persuade Clara to stop protecting Malcolm. Henry agreed with the first two. On the third, he said he had tried. Clara still called Malcolm her husband. She said fear had driven him and that exposing him would turn the entire family into gossip for other people's cocktail parties.

Daniel looked around the drawing room. Tonight's guests had become precisely that audience. Ruth addressed the outsiders and said this should not happen tonight. The two men near the hall exchanged a glance. One said they ought to leave, and Daniel turned toward them.

For a moment Daniel wanted them to go and carry the scandal into private clubs, offices and dinner parties. Let the Mercer name lose its mask of marble, silver and respectable charity. Yet something held him back—not pride, perhaps only exhaustion.

He told the men they did not need to flee his home as if they had witnessed an illegal transaction. Henry released a faint, bitter laugh. "Not yet," Daniel added. Ruth's look held both warning and relief. Daniel faced the remaining guests and announced that dinner was over. No one objected.

In suffocating embarrassment, guests collected their coats. A woman Daniel barely knew kissed Evelyn's cheek and offered a useless consolation. The investors retrieved their phones from the hall table. Servants moved expertly around the edges of the room, clearing abandoned glasses with the practiced ease of people accustomed to watching wealthy families fall apart.

Within fifteen minutes the estate was almost silent. Only Daniel, Ruth, Evelyn, Henry and one of the men from the hall remained. Daniel had asked him to stay. Mark Ellison was no friend, merely a potential business partner, but he understood trusts, debt and the quiet violence hidden inside inheritance. Daniel needed a witness. The gray-haired man stood beside the fireplace with his hands in his pockets and told Daniel to call a lawyer immediately—tonight.

Henry's phone vibrated again and he ignored it. Ruth took the black bag, sat beside Evelyn and lifted out the watch. Near the hinge was a tiny dent. Evelyn stared at it and said she had made it at twelve, when Clara let her hold the watch and she dropped it on the bathroom tile. She had cried for an hour.

The mark was nearly invisible unless one knew where to look. Something inside Daniel gave way—not relief, which was too generous a word, but the collapse of a frame that had held up half his life. His father was a liar. Henry was also a liar. His mother had known and chosen fear and silence. Daniel himself had spent years playing the devoted son who would never again ignore a family crisis.
## Chapter Six: Why Bring It Back Now?

He had never considered how many truths he had ignored. His phone showed a photo from earlier that evening: Daniel and Henry smiling beneath the chandelier, before the slap, the blood and the return of the watch. He nearly laughed, then put the phone away.

He asked why Henry had chosen now. Henry, still in his jacket despite the blow, said the estate was being appraised. Three weeks earlier he had learned Daniel intended to mortgage it again. Daniel said he was saving the foundation. Henry answered that he was preserving only its appearance.

Henry said Daniel was fighting to preserve a house that had spent a century devouring his family. Daniel advanced, but Ruth stood and stopped him. She told Henry he had no right to disappear for eighteen years and return speaking down to Daniel without knowing what her husband had sacrificed. Henry accepted that.

Then she turned on Daniel. "And you—stop using him as a substitute for your damned father because admitting what you are afraid of is harder." The words cut because they were true. Ruth had watched Daniel endure meetings he hated, flatter men who treated the Mercer name as a monument, sell two properties, cancel bonuses and postpone repairs while assuring Evelyn everything would be fine. He was not saving the foundation. He was trying to keep the estate from becoming proof of his father's complete failure.

Henry said the appraisal would uncover the old trust records. Once that happened, the watch could no longer remain hidden. Daniel accused him of protecting himself. Henry said yes, with a naked honesty that left Daniel's anger nowhere to land. But he had also returned to protect Daniel—from discovering the truth only after pledging everything he owned.

Daniel looked at Mark, whose expression supplied the answer he did not speak. Money removed from a trust did not vanish with time. It had become a concealed liability, one capable of consuming the estate, the foundation, the family name and everything Daniel had held together with favors and loans.

After a long silence, Evelyn rose with the watch. Daniel expected her to hand it to him, but she offered it to Henry. He refused to take it. She did not want it either. It was Clara's, she said—not Daniel's, not Malcolm's and not Henry's merely because they were the ones standing beside the wreckage now.

Evelyn set it on the glass table, where the gold reflected the chandelier. She wanted the entire truth, including the parts that could destroy their name. Mark warned that the road would be difficult. Evelyn answered that the night had already been difficult. Ruth almost smiled. Daniel sat for the first time since Henry arrived, and the soft beige sofa felt strangely unsafe.
## Chapter Seven: After the Performance Ended

Daniel noticed small things: champagne on the floor, a gold trace of wine on a glass, Ruth's bare left foot after removing one heel, and Henry's loosened collar. They were details people saw only after the performance was over.

"Play the rest," Daniel ordered. Henry hesitated. Daniel reminded him that he had come with the truth. Ruth passed him the phone. The second recording was shorter, and the first voice was Clara's. Daniel had not heard her so clearly in years. He had birthday messages and old reminders to buy tomatoes, but this was her exhausted voice near the end of her life.

"Henry," Clara said, "you cannot keep protecting him because you feel guilty." A younger Henry insisted he was trying to protect her. Clara answered that he was protecting the version of himself who had failed to see Malcolm at the beginning.

She told him to take the watch, hide it safely and never sell it. Malcolm must never touch it. When the children were grown, Henry was to tell them what they had all done. Not what Malcolm had done, or Henry had done—what we did. Clara, too, carried part of the crime. Perhaps she signed without reading, accepted impossible explanations out of love, or simply became too tired to resist. Daniel wanted to hate her, but could picture only the frayed cuff of her blue robe.
The recording ended. Evelyn sank onto the sofa. Tears brightened Henry's eyes but did not fall. Daniel asked why he had said nothing even after Malcolm died. Henry took a long time to answer.

He had hated Malcolm for dragging him into the crime, turning him into an accomplice, and leaving Clara to carry the ruin. Most of all, he hated that Malcolm had died before anyone could make him pay. Looking at Daniel and Evelyn afterward, Henry had resented their right to mourn a loving father and keep his perfect image. He had wanted that image to rot slowly inside them. The words were cruel and completely honest.

Ruth looked away. Evelyn stared at the watch. Daniel rose more slowly than before and thanked Henry. When Henry looked up in shock, Daniel raised a hand. It was not forgiveness—not tonight. Henry understood.

Daniel closed his hand around the watch. The metal was cold. For a second he wanted to claim it as Clara once had, carry it upstairs and lock it with the old silver and unopened letters. Instead, he returned it to the black bag and turned to Mark. He would cooperate fully with the trust lawyers and their investigation.
## Chapter Eight: The Cost of the Truth

Mark asked whether Daniel understood that cooperation might cost him the house. Daniel looked at the pale walls, ornamental plaster, crystal lights and polished floors that had witnessed weddings, funerals, Christmas dinners, arguments, fragile reconciliations and hundreds of long silences.

For a year he had treated the estate like a living body he had to save. Perhaps it was alive. Perhaps that was the problem. He said yes. Ruth came close enough for him to feel the warmth of her shoulder without taking his hand. Evelyn asked what would happen to the foundation. Mark said it depended on what the records revealed. "Then uncover all of them," she replied.

Henry picked up his phone, uncertain for the first time since entering. There were more documents, he warned, and they would hurt. Daniel had already guessed as much. In the yellow light left behind by the ruined dinner, the two men faced each other across the table.

Daniel's cheek ached from clenching his jaw. Henry's lip still bled. The music had stopped, the guests were gone and unfinished champagne warmed on the tables. Nothing had been repaired: Malcolm and Clara were still dead, the money remained gone, and the estate might still be lost.

Yet the lie over the family had changed its shape. It was no longer something Daniel could blame safely from across the room. Ruth asked what he intended to do with the watch. For now, Daniel said, no one would touch it. Henry agreed.

Evelyn gave a short laugh that became a sob and then another laugh. Clara, she said, would have hated Daniel's solution. He almost laughed too. "She hated nearly all my solutions." For the first time that night, remembering his mother's voice no longer felt like being attacked with it.
Daniel told Henry to stay—not because he trusted him, but because Henry would help them untangle every account. Henry glanced toward the foyer and said he doubted Daniel wanted him in the house.

Daniel surveyed the grand estate and its expensive decay, finally looking up at the chandelier suspended over them like a judgment. "I don't," he said. "But I am tired of deciding what I want before I know the truth." Henry lowered his eyes, pulled out a chair and sat opposite him.
Ruth divided the last champagne in the bottle among four glasses. No one proposed a toast. They drank anyway.
zh: ## 第一章：水晶灯下的耳光
清脆的耳光声在客厅里骤然炸响，Daniel Mercer 这一巴掌力道极大，甚至让周遭酒杯碰撞的轻音瞬间冻结。
这一击让 Henry Vale 的脸猛地偏向一侧。他踉跄了一下，肩膀重重磕在象牙白色的沙发边缘。有那么一秒钟，他半蜷缩在那里，单手死死撑着布艺靠背，头顶的水晶吊灯因这番动静而微微摇晃。
Daniel 居高临下地站在他面前，那身考究的米色西装衬托着他因愤怒而粗重的呼吸。
“你拿走了根本不属于你的家族遗物！”
全场鸦雀无声。
这间宽敞的客厅原本是为了举办一场奢华晚宴而布置的，随便拍张照都能溢出昂贵的质感。摇曳的烛光给米白色的墙壁镀上一层暖晕，远处的餐厅里隐约飘来弦乐四重奏的悠扬旋律。深色调的地板将浅色地毯衬托得格外亮眼，而那张镶金边的咖啡桌，正将头顶的水晶灯倒映成无数细碎的光斑。
在 Henry 身后不远处的走廊边缘，站着两名西装革履的男人，他们手中的酒杯已经默默放下。就在五分钟前，这两人还在高谈阔论 Mercer 基金会的未来。而现在，他们的表情仿佛在懊悔，当初代客泊车的门童递上车钥匙时，自己怎么没直接开车走人。
Evelyn Mercer 僵直地坐在米色沙发上，香槟色的晚礼服随着她的紧绷而现出褶皱，她手里依然攥着那只早已停止啜饮的酒杯。坐在她旁边的，是 Daniel 的妻子 Ruth，她的酒杯安静地搁在腿上，似乎整个人已经出神。
Henry 缓缓地直起了身子。
他的鼻下渗出了血迹。并不多，只在左侧上唇的边缘，挂着一抹暗红而刺眼的微光。
Daniel 垂在身侧的拳头依然紧握着。
Henry 并没有举手防御，更没有还击。他只是静静地注视着 Daniel，眼神中透着一种疲惫的从容——那是一个长年累月等待着某扇门被推开、并早已准备好迎接门后丑陋之物的人才会有的眼神。
“你其实可以直接问我的。” Henry 终于开口。
Daniel 发出一声短促的冷笑，声音干涩且极不自然。
“我十九岁那年就问过！而你当时告诉我，这不关我的事。”
“确实不关你的事。”
“那是属于我母亲的手表。”
Henry 的视线稍微低垂了半秒。那并非出于心虚，而更像是一种对往事的确认。
紧接着，Daniel 注意到了咖啡桌旁地毯上的那个黑色礼品袋。
它刚才绝对不在那里。
袋子的提手质地偏硬，是那种高级珠宝商常用的款式，意在让外包装看起来和里面的商品一样分量十足。袋口露出了白色的雪梨纸，而在纸张之下，一抹金色的反光正巧捕捉到了吊灯的余晖。
Daniel 的喉咙猛地发紧。
Henry 动作谨慎地弯下腰，他的膝盖似乎远比他平时愿意承认的要僵硬得多。他伸手够到那个袋子，将它从地毯上提了起来。
里面的物件在雪梨纸间发出轻微的摩擦声。
那是金子。圆润的轮廓。带着一种令 Daniel 深恶痛绝的熟悉感。
Marlowe 怀表。
在过去的十八年里，这块表在 Daniel 的脑海中一直是一个缺失的拼图，代表着家族里所有人都不愿诚实面对的那个夜晚。他母亲的生日晚宴。窗外狂风暴雨的拍打声。Henry Vale 外套扣子都没扣好就从厨房后门匆匆离开的背影。还有他父亲站在走廊里，嘴唇煞白、紧紧抿成一条直线的模样。
到了第二天早晨，手表就不翼而飞了。
而到了正午，Henry 就被钉在了窃贼的耻辱柱上。
Daniel 的父亲只把这件事说了一次，语气平静得像是在通知管家家里的水管爆裂了一样。
是 Henry 拿走的。
仅此而已。
## 第二章：那份档案
没有报警记录。没有向保险公司理赔。没有任何人能拿出实质性的对质证据。这个故事就像旧家具上的灰尘，在这个家里悄然落定，再也没有被拂去。
Henry 将那个礼品袋稳稳地放在了咖啡桌上，随后将手伸进了他的藏青色西装内侧。
Daniel 充满戒备地向前迈了一步。
然而 Henry 抽出的手心里，握着的只是一部手机。
“别乱来。” Daniel 警告道。
Henry 用大拇指抹去唇边的血迹。他盯着手指看了片刻，随后将手机举到耳边。
“把那份文件发过来。就现在。”
他的声音低沉而平稳。
Daniel 死死盯着他。
宴会的氛围似乎开始以碎片化的方式回溯。有人呼吸声稍微粗重了些；身后某处传来了玻璃杯相碰的脆响；餐厅里的音乐在一个乐句的中间突兀地戛然而止。
“什么文件？” Daniel 质问。
Henry 听着电话那头的声音，没有立刻回答。随后，他放下手臂，将手机滑回了口袋。
“你总是口口声声说想要真相，” 他开口道，“但你想要的，不过是一个能让你觉得双手依然干净的定制版本罢了。”
Daniel 的脸色变了。
Ruth 比任何人都更早察觉到了这一点。她认识 Daniel 太久了，久到足以捕捉到他愤怒面具下那一丝细微的裂痕——那是恐惧趁虚而入、让他的双眼瞬间凝滞的时刻。
“你今晚就是来羞辱我们的。” Daniel 咬着牙说。
Henry 将目光投向走廊，看向那两个穿深色西装的男人。一个是来自芝加哥的风投大佬，另一个则是 Daniel 苦心经营了六个月之久的保护信托基金董事会主席。他们的资金是保住 Mercer 庄园免遭拍卖的唯一希望，他们的点头能让 Daniel 勉强再撑上一年。
“我之所以挑在这个时候来，是因为你把那些最需要知道你父亲当年做了什么的人，请来了一大半。”
Daniel 的身体瞬间变得僵硬无比。
Evelyn 放下香槟杯的动作太急，几滴酒液溅落在了桌面上。
“我爸爸到底做了什么？” 她颤声问道。
她的声音微弱得完全不像 Daniel 记忆中的妹妹。
Henry 看向她，眼神里的某些东西不自觉地柔和了下来。
“别在这里说。” 他轻声回答。
Daniel 猛地逼近一步，直到两人之间只隔着那张咖啡桌。
“不，就在这儿说！”
Ruth 从沙发上站起身。她黑色的裙摆轻轻扫过靠垫。她并没有伸手去触碰 Daniel，因为她深知，在这个男人正拼命证明自己能够独自承受一切的时候，最好不要去拉扯他。
“Daniel。” 她轻柔地唤了一声。
他没有回头看她。
Henry 的手机震动了一下。
他低头瞥了一眼，下颌的肌肉瞬间收紧。
接着，他将手机放在了玻璃桌面上，正好位于那个黑色袋子和几杯喝剩的香槟之间。
“自己看吧。” 他说。
Daniel 的视线落在了屏幕上。
那是一封带有附件的邮件。没有博人眼球的标题，没有复杂的加密文件夹。只有一个扫描文件，以及一个音频附件。
最先被点开的是那份文件。
一本信托账簿。
Daniel 对家族财务的了解，足以让他一眼认出抬头那古老的 Mercer 家族信托标志。他父亲生前几乎在所有东西上都印着这个，甚至是去超市的购物清单。纸张边缘已经泛黄，名字是用蓝黑色的墨水打印上去的。
Malcolm Mercer。
Henry Vale。
Clara Mercer。
——Daniel 的母亲。
他感觉到自己的呼吸声开始变得遥远。
这一页记录着一笔从 Clara Mercer 家族信托向一个 Daniel 闻所未闻的私人账户转账的明细。那个惊人的数字让他的胃忍不住痉挛起来。
Evelyn 走到他身边，停下脚步。
“那是……什么？” 她用气声问道。
Daniel 仿佛失语了一般。
回答她的是 Henry。
“你父亲在三年间陆陆续续掏空了这笔钱。他用一部分去填补债务窟窿，用一部分去给公司续命，还有一部分……仅仅是因为他太骄傲，无法接受早在别人察觉之前，这个家族就已经不再富有的事实。”
Daniel 猛地抬起头。
“你以为我会相信你的鬼话？”
## 第三章：蓝黑墨水里的三个名字
“不。” Henry 的嘴角抽动了一下，尽管毫无笑意，“我预料到你会恨我。恨我，对你来说一直是一件很容易的事。”
Ruth 向桌子走近了几步，她的视线在账簿和 Henry 的脸上来回梭巡。
“那为什么上面会有你的名字？” 她尖锐地指出。
Henry 缓缓吸了一口气。
“因为第一笔转账，是我签的字。”
全场死寂。
那时的他，是他们父亲的首席财务官，是父亲的挚友。是那个在 Daniel 大学毕业时送他一本皮面日记本，并郑重告诫他不要成为那种“将金钱与权力混为一谈”的男人。
Daniel 曾经深深敬仰过他。
或许正因如此，后来的恨意才会如此刻骨铭心。
“你是他的帮凶。” Daniel 从牙缝里挤出这句话。
“没错。”
这句肯定的回答，比任何辩解都显得更具杀伤力。
Henry 将手伸进礼品袋，拨开了那层白色的雪梨纸。
那块怀表静静地躺在里面。
它看起来比 Daniel 记忆中要小一些。纯金质地，椭圆形的表盘，配着圆润的翻盖，边缘缠绕着一根极细的金链。在 Daniel 出生前几十年，他祖母的首字母就已经被镌刻在了表背上。这块金属依然散发着老钱家族特有的温润光泽——那种历经战争、离婚、投资失败后，依然让拥有它的人坚信自己的姓氏能够不朽的光泽。
他的母亲每次出远门，都会把它放在大衣口袋里。
Daniel 至少还记得这些。
他记得童年时，母亲在早餐桌旁打开它的情景。那微弱的滴答声。以及她每次听到这声音时嘴角泛起的微笑，尽管她从未解释过原因。
“它本来是要被卖掉的。” Henry 打破了沉默。
Daniel 的目光瞬间如刀般射向他。
Henry 微微点了点头。
“你父亲找好了一个买家。是日内瓦的某个人。这笔钱原本可以再替他掩盖一轮债务，让他能再多争取一点时间，去假装一切安然无恙。”
“所以你捷足先登，把它拿走了。”
“对，我拿走了。”
Evelyn 发出了一声奇怪的动静，听起来像是介于嗤笑与抽泣之间的声音。
Daniel 的手死死抠住桌子的边缘。
“所以，你终究还是个小偷。”
Henry 凝视了他很久。
“我赶在 Malcolm 卖掉它之前，从保险箱里拿走了它。是你母亲求我这么做的。”
这句话一出，房间里的空气都随之扭曲了。
氛围并没有变得更安静，而是变得更加危险。
Daniel 花了整整十八年的时间，才将过去的往事拼凑成一个他能够独自背负的形状：Henry 是贼，父亲是为了挽救家族的英雄，母亲是无辜的受害者，而自己当年只是无能为力。
简单的故事，总是更容易让人活下去。
但这，一点都不简单。
“我母亲求你拿走的？” 他一字一顿地问。
“她早就知道信托基金被动了手脚。”
“那她为什么不告诉我们？！”
“她尝试过。”
Henry 的视线缓缓移到了手机屏幕的文件上。
“你父亲说她脑子糊涂了。他说那些药物影响了她的记忆力，说她只是太累了。他对医生这么说，对律师这么说，对着每一个觉得相信他更省事的人这么说。”
Ruth 转头看向 Evelyn。
Evelyn 已经面如死灰。
他们的母亲那段时间确实病了。虽然还没到弥留之际，但却疲惫得让年轻的 Daniel 无法理解。她会把窗帘半拉着，在楼上的起居室里度过漫长的下午。她开始记不住名字。当 Daniel 晚归错过晚餐时，她会哭泣着道歉，仿佛只是不小心把红酒洒在了地毯上。
那时的他才二十岁，他只觉得母亲很脆弱。
他不知道的是，一个人的脆弱，是可以被硬生生制造出来的。
“你就这么眼睁睁看着他作践她？” Daniel 怒吼。
Henry 的表情痛苦地绷紧了。
“一开始我是帮着他的。我用‘我们是为了不让她受刺激’来麻痹自己。我一直用这个借口催眠自己，直到我自己都觉得恶心。”
“后来呢？”
## 第四章：他唯一救下的东西
“后来，我就拿走了那块表。”
“这就是你给出的反击？”
“那是我唯一能在不引发财务审计的情况下，拿走的东西。”
Daniel 就这么瞪着他。
直到这一刻，Henry 的声音里才第一次透出了锋利。
“你觉得我当年很英勇吗？不，我根本不勇敢。我怕他。我怕失去这份工作。我也怕如果你母亲知道了我瞒了她那么久，她会崩溃。所以我偷了那块表，我把它藏了起来，我骗自己说，我至少保住了一点东西。”
他的目光垂向那件金色的物件。
“我保住了一块该死的手表。”
这句话如同巨石般砸在两人之间。
在走廊后方，其中一位投资人默默地放下了酒杯。
没有人请他离开。
也没有人请任何人离开。
这就是富人圈子里派对最可怕的地方。当灾难发生时，人们学会了保持绝对的静止。他们擅长在把自己变成透明人的同时，把一切细节尽收眼底。
Daniel 拿起了手机。
那个音频文件就躺在账簿文档的下方。
他按下了播放键。
一开始只有电流的沙沙声。
随后，他父亲的声音传了出来。
Malcolm Mercer 已经离世十四个月了，但 Daniel 一瞬间就认出了那个音色。那标志性的、略带刻薄的耐心。那种带着疲态的优越感。那种连道歉听起来都像是在纠正别人错误的语气。
“我需要你把表拿走。” Malcolm 在录音里说。
另一个声音回应了。是 Henry，更年轻，也更尖锐。
“她会发现的。”
“她现在对什么都疑神疑鬼。这才是最大的麻烦。”
“你不能卖掉它。”
“我自己的东西，我想怎么处置就怎么处置。”
“那不是你的东西。”
录音里陷入了短暂的沉默。
接着，Malcolm 笑了。并不大声，甚至听起来有些和蔼。
“你领我的薪水都十五年了，Henry。别在这个时候跟我谈什么原则。”
录音戛然而止。
餐厅里，一把椅子在地板上发出了极其轻微的摩擦声。
Daniel 的手指死死抠着手机边缘，直到 Ruth 伸手将它拿走。
她并没有出声安慰他。她接管手机，仅仅是因为他攥得快要把屏幕捏碎了。
Evelyn 颓然跌坐回沙发上。
金色的裙摆在她膝盖周围堆叠开来。此时的她看起来比 Daniel 要年轻得多，尽管他们之间其实只差了三岁。
“我记得她问过这块表。” 她喃喃自语。
Daniel 猛地转头。
她的声音飘得很远，并没有在对任何人说话。
“那天晚上妈妈来到了我的房间。她穿着那件袖口已经磨破的蓝色睡袍。她问我有没有看到爸爸。我说他在楼下。然后她说，‘如果 Henry 来了，千万别让你哥哥觉得他做错了什么。’”
Daniel 闭上了眼睛。
Evelyn 用手捂住了嘴。
“我以为她指的是关于晚餐安排的事……我以为……我不知道我当时到底是怎么想的。”
“你那时才十七岁。” Ruth 轻声宽慰道。
Evelyn 抬头看向 Henry。
“你明明知道我们都会恨你。”
“是的。”
“而你就这么让我们恨了十八年。”
“是的。”
这是今晚，Henry 第一次显露出真正的老态。
不是那种体面的老去。不是他平时走进董事会时，带着精心打理的银发、闪亮的袖扣，用让银行家都不自觉坐直的声音说话时的那种从容的老去。
而是纯粹的、油尽灯枯的疲惫。
“我妻子当时病得很重，” 他缓缓说道，“我不是在找借口，这只是个事实。我已经答应过她，我会把一切都处理好。我原本以为，如果我能把表弄出那栋房子，阻止 Malcolm 卖掉它，我之后就能带着确凿的证据回来。我以为我能把一切都清理干净。”
他低头看了看大拇指上沾染的血迹。
“但没有什么是干净的。”
Daniel 强忍着想再给他一拳的冲动。
这股怒火来得如此猛烈，以至于他的身体都微微前倾了。
但他最终只是死死抓住了椅背。
Henry 就这么静静地看着他克制自己。
## 第五章：克拉拉最害怕的观众
“你当年就该把一切告诉我们。” Daniel 咬牙切齿地说。
“我本该这么做。”
“你本该去报警！”
“我本该去。”
“你本该劝我母亲不要再包庇那个混蛋！”
“我劝了。”
这句话让 Daniel 瞬间哑火。
Henry 的表情变得有些扭曲。
“她根本听不进去。她说 Malcolm 依然是她的丈夫。她说他只是太害怕了。她甚至说，如果我曝光了他，你们整个家族就会沦为别人酒会上的笑柄和谈资。”
Daniel 的目光扫过整个客厅。
而今晚的宾客，已经完美地充当了这群观众。
Ruth 捕捉到了他脸上一闪而过的神情。
“不该是今晚。” 她对着其他外人说道。
她的声音虽然不大，却带着不容置疑的分量。
站在走廊附近的那两个男人对视了一眼。
其中一人开口了：“我们该走了。”
Daniel 转过身，面向他们。
有那么一瞬间，他想任由他们离开。让他们把这个丑闻带回这座城市，带进他们的私人俱乐部、高级办公室和晚宴上。让 Mercer 这个姓氏，彻底撕下那层由大理石、银器和体面慈善伪装的面具，露出它本来的面目。
但内心深处的某种东西拉扯住了他。
并非出于骄傲。
也许仅仅是因为疲惫。
“不。” Daniel 出声阻拦。
那两个人停下了脚步。
“这是我的家，” 他继续说道，“你们没必要弄得好像撞见了什么非法交易一样仓皇逃窜。”
Henry 发出了一声微弱而苦涩的轻笑。
Daniel 回头瞥了他一眼。
“现在还没到那一步。” 他补充道。
Ruth 的目光迅速扫向他，眼神中交织着警告与释然。
Daniel 重新转回身，面对着剩余的客人。
“晚宴到此结束。” 他宣布，“感谢各位今晚的光临。”
没有人提出异议。
人们在令人窒息的尴尬中纷纷拿回自己的外套。一位 Daniel 几乎叫不出名字的女士，上前吻了吻 Evelyn 的脸颊，低声留下一句无关痛痒的安慰。那两位投资人从走廊的桌子上取回了各自的手机。佣人们则极其默契地在房间边缘穿梭，手脚麻利地收走被遗弃的酒杯——这种熟练的姿态，仿佛他们早就见惯了富贵人家的分崩离析。
不到十五分钟，整座宅邸便陷入了几乎死寂的状态。
硕大的空间里，只剩下 Daniel、Ruth、Evelyn、Henry，以及之前站在走廊里的其中一个男人。
是 Daniel 要求他留下来的。
他们算不上朋友，甚至可以说毫无交情。他们充其量只是潜在的商业伙伴。但这些懂得操纵数字、信托、债务，并深谙遗产继承背后那无声暴力的老手，正是 Daniel 此刻需要的。他留下他，不是出于信任，而是需要一个见证人。
这个名叫 Mark Ellison 的灰发男人，此刻正双手插兜站在壁炉旁。
“你现在应该立刻联系律师。” Mark 给出建议。
“我会的。” Daniel 回答。
“就在今晚。”
“我说了，我会的。”
Henry 的手机再次震动起来。
但他视若无睹。
Ruth 从咖啡桌上拿起那个黑色礼品袋，走到沙发旁。她在 Evelyn 身边坐下，小心翼翼地剥开雪梨纸，取出了那块怀表。
在靠近铰链的地方，有一个极不显眼的凹痕。
Evelyn 盯着它看。
“那是我弄出来的。” 她喃喃道。
Daniel 侧过头。
“十二岁那年，妈妈让我拿着它玩，结果我手滑把它掉在了浴室的瓷砖上。我当时足足哭了一个小时。”
Ruth 轻轻将怀表翻转过来。
那个凹痕实在太小了，如果不是事先知道，根本无从察觉。
Daniel 感觉到胸腔里有什么东西突然松懈了下来。不是释然，用“释然”来形容太过奢侈。那更像是一种支撑了他半辈子的架子被瞬间抽走的感觉。
他的父亲是个骗子。
Henry 也是个骗子。
而他的母亲，虽然知情，却选择了恐惧与沉默。
至于 Daniel 自己？他将半生都塑造成了那个“绝不会再对家族危机视而不见”的孝子形象。
## 第六章：为什么现在带回来
他甚至都没意识到，自己曾经无视了多少真相。
口袋里的手机震动了一下。是他首席运营官发来的消息。附带的是今晚早些时候拍的一张照片：Daniel 站在水晶吊灯下，与 Henry Vale 并肩而立，面带微笑。那是在那一记耳光之前，在鲜血流出之前，在那块表重见天日之前。
Daniel 差一点就笑出声来。
但他只是默默地把手机塞回了口袋。
“为什么偏偏选在现在把表带回来？” 他转头质问 Henry。
Henry 依然站在咖啡桌旁。
他甚至都没有脱下西装外套。即便挨了 Daniel 一拳之后也没有。
“因为这栋房子正在进行资产评估。” Henry 平静地说。
“这算什么狗屁理由？”
“确实不算。”
Henry 仰起头看了一眼天花板，又将视线落回 Daniel 身上。
“三周前，我得知你正准备拿这片庄园去再次抵押贷款。”
Daniel 的咬肌瞬间绷紧了。
“我是为了拯救基金会！”
“你只是为了保住基金会表面的风光。”
“你对我们现在所做的事情一无所知。”
“我只知道，你正拼尽全力去维护一栋在过去一百年里，一直在生吞活剥你整个家族的破房子。”
Daniel 怒气冲冲地朝他逼近了一步。
Ruth 猛地站起身。
“够了！”
Daniel 停住了脚步。
她的声音虽然不大，却透着冰冷的坚决。
她将矛头转向 Henry。
“你没有资格在消失了十八年后突然出现，用这种高高在上的口吻对他指手画脚。你根本不知道他为了支撑这个家付出了多大的代价。”
Henry 垂下头，点了点头。
“你说的对。”
随后，Ruth 转身盯住了 Daniel。
“还有你。不要因为承认自己内心的恐惧太难，就把他当成你那个该死的父亲来发泄。”
Daniel 怔怔地看着她。
这句话之所以如此刺痛，正是因为它残忍地揭开了真相。
在过去的一年里，Ruth 默默看着他出入那些他极其厌恶的会议室，看着他与那些把 Mercer 家族的名字当作某种亟待保护的历史遗迹的人虚与委蛇。她看着他变卖了两处房产，取消了员工的奖金，推迟了庄园的修缮，然后转过头去，用一种极其自信的口吻告诉 Evelyn 一切都会好起来——那种盲目的自信，曾无数次让她想把杯子砸在他脸上。
他根本不是在拯救什么基金会。
他只是在拼命阻止这栋大宅沦为他父亲彻底失败的铁证。
Henry 再次开口了。
“我把表带回来，是因为这次的资产评估绝对会查出当年信托基金的账目。一旦事情败露，我就再也藏不住它了。”
Daniel 眯起了眼睛。
“所以归根结底，你还是为了自保。”
“是的。”
这种近乎赤裸的坦诚，反而让 Daniel 的怒火失去着力点。
Henry 继续说道：
“但我也是为了保护你。”
“保护我什么？”
“保护你，免得你在把所有东西都抵押出去之后，才发现这一切。”
Daniel 把目光投向了 Mark Ellison。
Mark 一言不发。他也无需多言。他脸上的表情已经说明了一切。
当年信托基金里不翼而飞的钱，并没有随着时间长河彻底消散。
它已经变成了一笔隐形的负债。
一笔足以在今天随时引爆的负债。
这笔负债足以吞噬这座庄园、基金会、家族的声誉，以及 Daniel 一直以来用人情和借款勉强维系的所有脆弱的一切。
房间里陷入了漫长的死寂。
片刻后，Evelyn 从沙发上站起身，手里紧紧捏着那块怀表。
她朝 Daniel 走去。
Daniel 以为她要把表交给他。
然而，她却转了个方向，将表递到了 Henry 面前。
Henry 并没有伸手去接。
“我不想要它。” Evelyn 声音有些发颤。
Daniel 震惊地看着她。
## 第七章：表演结束以后
“不。” 她的眼眶泛红，但目光却毫不退缩，“这是妈妈的遗物。它不属于你。不属于爸爸。也不属于他。” 她朝着 Henry 扬了扬下巴。“更不能仅仅因为我们是现在唯一站在这堆烂摊子旁边的人，它就理所当然地属于我们。”
Ruth 注视着她，眼神中流露出一丝异样的骄傲。
Evelyn 决绝地将怀表放在了玻璃桌面上。
金色的表壳反射着头顶华丽的吊灯光芒。
“我只想知道到底发生了什么。” 她一字一顿地说，“全部的真相。哪怕是那些会让我们家族彻底身败名裂的部分。”
一直站在壁炉旁的 Mark 微微动了动身子。
“那将会是一条非常艰难的路。” 他提醒道。
Evelyn 给了他一个疲惫至极的眼神。
“今晚也很艰难。”
Ruth 的嘴角微微上扬，勾起一个难以察觉的弧度。
Daniel 终于坐了下来，这是自 Henry 闯入以来的第一次。
他突然觉得这米色的沙发软得让人毫无安全感。
他开始注意到一些细枝末节：桌子旁边地板上有一抹淡淡的香槟酒渍，玻璃杯边缘挂着一丝金色的水痕；Ruth 脱掉了一只高跟鞋，光着左脚踩在地毯上；而 Henry 衬衫的领口也已经散开了。
都是些微不足道的小事。
却只有当所有伪装的戏码落幕后，人们才有精力去察觉它们。
“把剩下的录音放完。” Daniel 吩咐道。
Henry 僵在原地。
Daniel 抬头直视他。
“你自己说的，你带着真相而来。”
Henry 点了点头。
Ruth 将手机递给 Daniel。
第二段音频的时间更短。
最先响起的，是他母亲的声音。
Daniel 已经很多年没有听过她这么清晰的嗓音了。他手里当然存着一些录音，比如生日时的语音留言，或者让他顺路从市场带几个番茄回家的旧语音。但这不一样。这是她生命最后阶段那种透支了的、疲倦至极的声音。
“Henry，” 她虚弱地开口，“你不能因为内疚，就无休止地包庇他。”
一阵沉默。
接着是 Henry 的声音，依然是那个年轻的版本：“我是在努力保护你。”
“不。” 录音里的她深吸了一口气。“你只是在努力保护那个，一开始没看清他真面目的你自己。”
Daniel 觉得自己的喉咙像被什么东西死死掐住了。
母亲的声音继续传来：
“如果你拿走了那块表，把它藏在安全的地方。别卖掉它。绝不能让 Malcolm 碰它。等孩子们都长大了，告诉他们，我们当年都做了什么。”
我们 做了什么。
不是 Malcolm 做了什么。
不是 Henry 做了什么。
是 我们。
他的母亲，同样背负了这桩罪恶的一部分。
也许她曾经在没有细看的情况下就签了字；也许她出于对丈夫的爱，选择了盲目接受那些荒谬的解释；也许她只是太累了，失去了反抗的力气。
Daniel 多想去恨她。
但他脑海中浮现的，只有她那件蓝色睡袍上磨损的袖口。
录音结束了。
Evelyn 瘫坐回原位。
Henry 的眼底闪烁着水光，但他强忍着没有让眼泪掉下来。
“我父亲死的时候，你为什么什么都不说？” Daniel 质问道。
Henry 过了很久才回答。
“因为我恨他。” 他终于吐出这句话。
Daniel 愣住了。
Henry 的脸上浮现出一种近乎羞愧的神情。
“我恨他把我拖下水，强迫我成为共犯。我恨他把所有的烂摊子都推给你母亲来背。我更恨他竟然赶在任何人能让他付出代价之前，就自己先死了。当他死后，我看着你们兄妹俩，我心想，凭什么你们还能以一个慈父的名义去哀悼他？凭什么你们还能在心里保留他完美无瑕的形象？”
他艰难地咽了口唾沫。
“我就是要让那个完美的幻象，在你们心里慢慢腐烂。”
这些字眼如此恶毒，却又无比真实。
Ruth 别开了脸。
Evelyn 则呆呆地盯着那块表。
Daniel 再次站起身，动作比之前迟缓了许多。
“谢谢你。” 他低声说。
Henry 惊愕地抬起头。
Daniel 抬起一只手，打断了他可能的反驳。
“但别误会，这不是原谅。”
## 第八章：真相的代价
“我明白。”
“至少今晚不可能。”
“我懂。”
Daniel 径直走向桌子，将那块怀表握入掌心。
金属的触感冰冷彻骨。
有那么一秒钟，他甚至想学着母亲当年的样子，把它揣进自己的口袋里。紧紧贴着自己。宣示它的归属权。然后把它带上楼，锁进那个专门存放旧银器和无人拆阅的旧信件的家族保险箱里。
但他最终只是把它放回了那个黑色的礼品袋中。
随后，他转身看向 Mark Ellison。
“联系信托律师吧。” Daniel 语气平静，“告诉他们，我们会全力配合调查。”
Mark 审视着他。
“你清楚这意味着什么吗？”
“我很清楚。”
“这可能意味着你会失去这栋房子。”
Daniel 环顾四周。
米白色的墙壁、精致的石膏线脚、璀璨的水晶吊灯。还有这见证了无数场婚礼、葬礼、圣诞晚宴、激烈争吵、勉强和解，以及成百上千次漫长沉默的抛光地板。
过去的一整年里，他一直把这栋房子当成有生命的躯体一样，拼了命地去拯救它。
也许它确实是有生命的。
而也许，这才是问题的根源所在。
“是的。” 他给出了最终的回答。
Ruth 走过来，站在他身旁。
她没有牵他的手。只是靠得足够近，让他能真切地感受到她肩膀传来的温度。
Evelyn 深深地吸了一口气。
“那基金会会怎么样？” 她问。
Daniel 看向 Mark。
Mark 的回答十分谨慎。
“那得看最终能查出些什么账目。”
Evelyn 点了点头。
“那就把所有的账目都翻出来。”
Henry 拿起了他的手机。
自打他进门以来，这还是他第一次露出不确定的神情。
“还有其他的文件。” 他提醒道。
Daniel 迎上他的目光。
“我猜到了。”
“那些内容会非常伤人。”
“估计吧。”
Henry 默默地点了一下头。
在这场彻底搞砸的晚宴残留的昏黄灯光下，这两个男人隔着桌子对立着。
Daniel 脸颊的肌肉因为之前的用力咬合而依然隐隐作痛。Henry 的嘴唇还在渗着细微的血丝。音乐声早已停歇。宾客们散去无踪。周围桌上那些喝剩的香槟，正在室温下慢慢变暖。
什么都没有被解决。
他的父亲依然死了。
他的母亲依然不在了。
被挥霍的钱依然填不回来。
这栋房子最终可能依然保不住。
但那个盘踞在家族上空的谎言，已经彻底改变了形态。
它再也不是那个 Daniel 可以躲在房间另一头，心安理得地指责是别人的过错的东西了。
Ruth 看向那个黑色的礼品袋。
“你打算怎么处理它？” 她问。
Daniel 盯着袋子里的怀表。
“就目前来说？” 他反问。
他停顿了一下。
“就目前来说，谁都别碰它。”
Henry 微微点了点头表示同意。
Evelyn 突然短促地笑了一声，很轻。那笑声变成了一声抽泣，紧接着又是一声轻笑。
Daniel 疑惑地看着她。
“怎么了？”
她用手背抹了一下眼角。
“妈妈一定会讨厌你这个处理方式的。”
他差点就笑出声来。
“她几乎讨厌我所有的处理方式。”
“这倒也是。”
这是今晚 Daniel 第一次在回忆里听到母亲的声音时，不再觉得它像是某种被用来攻击自己的武器。
他转头看向 Henry。
“你留下来。” Daniel 命令道。
Henry 的表情瞬间僵硬了。
“不是因为我信任你，” Daniel 补充道，“而是因为，你得帮我们把这堆烂账一笔一笔地理清楚。”
Henry 朝门厅的方向瞥了一眼。
“我不确定你真的想让我在你家里待着。”
Daniel 环顾四周。看着这座宏伟的豪宅，看着它所承载的昂贵的腐朽，最后，他的目光落在了那盏如同审判般悬在所有人头顶的水晶吊灯上。
“是不想。” 他说，“但我已经受够了在搞清楚真相之前，就自作主张地去决定我到底想要什么。”
Henry 垂下了视线。
片刻之后，他拉开椅子，在 Daniel 的对面坐了下来。
Ruth 将瓶底最后一点香槟均匀地倒进了四个杯子里。
没有人提议干杯。
但他们还是将杯中酒一饮而尽。
